entry: Eukaryotic cell of green plants. Plant cells have a rigid primary wall of [[Cellulose|cellulose]], hemicelluloses and pectin, built outside the cell membrane. This composition differs from the chitin of fungal walls, the peptidoglycan of bacteria and the pseudopeptidoglycan of archaea. Plastids, most notably [[Chloroplast|chloroplasts]], contain chlorophyll and perform [[Photosynthesis|photosynthesis]], converting sunlight into chemical energy. Many cells contain a large central [[Vacuole|vacuole]] that maintains turgor pressure, stores materials and digests waste. Flagella and centrioles are absent except in the motile sperm of bryophytes, pteridophytes, cycads and *Ginkgo*. Cell division builds a cell plate with a phragmoplast, separating the daughter cells. Specialized cells differentiate from [[Meristem|meristematic cells]], which are analogous to animal stem cells.

Signal molecule produced within plants in very low concentrations. Plant hormones control embryogenesis, organ size, defense against pathogens, stress tolerance and reproductive development. Unlike animals, in which specialized glands produce hormones, each plant cell can produce them. The five classical classes are auxins, cytokinins, gibberellins, abscisic acid and [[Ethylene|ethylene]]. Only some cells respond, and they do so at specific points in their growth cycle. Hormones move by cytoplasmic streaming, diffusion and [[Vascular tissue|vascular tissue]], through which sugars travel from leaves to roots and flowers and water and minerals move from roots to foliage. Plants regulate hormone levels by storing or breaking them down, or by binding them to [[Carbohydrate|carbohydrates]], [[Amino acid|amino acids]] or [[Peptide|peptides]]. Natural and synthetic hormones are used in agriculture as plant growth regulators. Some microorganisms produce similar compounds, though these are better regarded as secondary metabolites.

Study of the physical form and external structure of plants. It is usually distinguished from [[Plant anatomy|plant anatomy]], which examines internal structure at the microscopic level, and it is useful for identifying plants visually. Morphologists compare structures across species. Structures that arise from common inherited pathways are homologous; for example, [[Cactus|cactus]] spines are homologous to leaves. The field studies vegetative structures, such as stems, leaves and roots, and reproductive ones, such as flowers, seeds, fern sori and moss capsules. Study of reproductive structures revealed the [[Alternation of generations|alternation of generations]] found in all plants and most algae. The field examines structure from ultrastructure to overall growth habit, and it studies how structures develop. Molecular studies have found transcriptome conservation patterns that mark key transitions in the plant life cycle. Johann Wolfgang von Goethe's *Metamorphosis of Plants* proposed an archetypal plant form.

Production of offspring by sexual or asexual means. [[Sexual reproduction|Sexual reproduction]] fuses gametes to produce offspring genetically different from either parent. Vegetative reproduction produces new individuals without gamete fusion, and these clones are genetically identical unless [[Mutation|mutations]] occur. In [[Asexual reproduction|asexual reproduction]] only one parent is involved, and the offspring inherit its characteristics. Asexual methods include budding, fragmentation, spore formation, regeneration and vegetative propagation. Perennial plants often reproduce vegetatively through modified stems or roots, forming clonal colonies that persist and expand. A disadvantage is that [[Pathogen|pathogens]] can pass from parent to offspring. Apomixis, the formation of seeds without fertilization, occurs in dandelions (*Taraxacum*), hawkweeds (*Hieracium*), some *Citrus* species and Kentucky bluegrass (*Poa pratensis*). Rhizomes and runners, or stolons, are important organs of vegetative reproduction.

Study of the form and structure of plant parts involved in sexual reproduction. Among living organisms, flowers, the reproductive structures of [[Flowering plant|flowering plants]], are the most physically varied. Non-flowering plants, including green algae, mosses, liverworts, hornworts, ferns and conifers, also have complex reproductive adaptations. The breeding system, which determines how sperm from one plant fertilizes the ovum of another, is the single most important determinant of genetic structure in nonclonal plant populations. Christian Konrad Sprengel studied pollination in 1793, and [[Charles Darwin]] used this work to build his theory of evolution. Plants alternate between a [[Sporophyte|sporophyte]] and a [[Gametophyte|gametophyte]] generation. In bryophytes the gametophyte dominates, while in ferns and seed plants the sporophyte dominates. Flowers are built from sepals and petals, stamens that produce [[Pollen|pollen]], and carpels bearing ovules.

One of two main structural axes of a vascular plant, the other being the root. The stem supports leaves, flowers and fruits, and transports water and dissolved substances between the roots and shoots. It also carries out photosynthesis, stores nutrients and produces new living tissue. Leaves attach at nodes, which may bear axillary buds that grow into branches, and the segments between nodes are internodes. Stems are usually aerial, though some are underground. Xylem moves water by transpiration pull, capillary action and root pressure, while phloem distributes food from photosynthetic tissue. Cambium lies between them. Stems are often specialized for storage or protection, including [[Onion|onion]] bulbs, [[Taro|taro]] corms and the flattened cladodes of [[Cactus|cactus]] pads.

Small, usually circular DNA molecule that replicates independently of chromosomal DNA. Plasmids are most commonly found in [[Bacteria|bacteria]] and [[Archaea|archaea]], though some occur in eukaryotes. They often carry genes for [[Antibiotic|antibiotic]] resistance, virulence, secondary metabolism and bioremediation, and they are usually much smaller than chromosomes. Artificial plasmids are widely used as vectors in [[Cloning|molecular cloning]] and are introduced into cells by transformation. Plasmids pass between bacteria mostly by conjugation, a route of horizontal gene transfer. Unlike [[Virus|viruses]], plasmids lack a protein capsid. They range from 1 to over 400 kbp in size, and a cell may hold from one to thousands of copies. Joshua Lederberg coined the term in 1952. In 1973 recombinant plasmids were constructed with restriction enzymes such as EcoRI, enabling the production of [[Insulin|insulin]].

Surgical specialty concerned with restoring, reconstructing or altering the body. It is divided into reconstructive surgery, which restores or improves the function of body parts and includes the treatment of burns, and cosmetic surgery, which aims solely to improve appearance. Because it has no distinct anatomical object, plastic surgery overlaps with nearly all other surgical specialties. The word *plastic* derives from the Greek *plastikē tekhnē*, "the art of modeling." The Edwin Smith papyrus (c. 1600 BC) describes treatment of a broken nose, and the *Sushruta Samhita* in India described nasal reconstruction using skin flaps. Gaspare Tagliacozzi of [[Bologna]] popularized rhinoplasty using a flap of skin from the patient's upper arm. Modern plastic surgery emerged during [[World War I]], when Harold Gillies developed skin grafting and flap techniques for facial injuries. Over 20 million cosmetic procedures are performed annually worldwide, and empirical data show variable psychological benefits, with risks including dissatisfaction and worsened [[Body dysmorphic disorder|body dysmorphic disorder]].

Permanent deformation of a solid material in response to applied forces. In engineering, the transition from elastic to plastic behavior is called yielding. Plastic deformation occurs in most materials, including [[Metal|metals]], soils, [[Rock (geology)|rocks]], [[Concrete|concrete]] and [[Foam|foams]], but its physical causes vary. In metals it results mainly from dislocations, and a pure metal deforms by slip or twinning. In brittle materials such as rock, concrete and bone, it is caused mainly by slip at microcracks, while in foams and biological tissues it arises from rearrangements of bubbles or cells. Most metals are more plastic when hot than when cold. Plasticity is directly proportional to the ductility and malleability of a material. Materials hardened by prior deformation, such as by cold forming, need higher stresses to deform further. The von Mises yield criterion predicts yielding in metals.

Membrane-bound organelle found in the cells of plants, algae and some other eukaryotes. Plastids are considered to derive from endosymbiotic cyanobacteria. Types include [[Chloroplast|chloroplasts]], which perform [[Photosynthesis|photosynthesis]]; chromoplasts, which synthesize and store pigments; and colorless leucoplasts. A primary endosymbiosis about 1.5 billion years ago gave rise to plastids in the Archaeplastida, including land plants, red algae, green algae and glaucophytes. Later secondary and tertiary endosymbioses occurred in many organisms, and some keep ingested plastids in a process called kleptoplasty. Andreas Schimper first named, described and defined plastids. In land plants, plastids derive from proplastids in [[Meristem|meristematic]] regions and can differentiate into forms such as amyloplasts, which store [[Starch|starch]] and help detect gravity, and elaioplasts, which store [[Fat|fats]]. Each plastid has its own genome, or plastome.

Genus of [[Tree|trees]] that are the sole living members of the family Platanaceae. Mature members reach 30–50 m (98–164 ft) in height. The type species is the Oriental plane (*Platanus orientalis*). All except *P. kerrii* are deciduous, and most grow in riparian or other [[Wetland|wetland]] habitats in the wild, though they tolerate drought in cultivation. The name plane derives from Latin *platanus*, from a Greek word that may relate to *platýs*, meaning broad, a reference to the broad leaves or flat bark. Some North American species are called sycamores, especially *P. occidentalis*. The flowers are wind-pollinated and borne in balls, and the fruit is a ball of achenes with bristles that aid wind dispersal. The bark peels off in irregular patches. The [[Hybrid (biology)|hybrid]] London plane (*P.* × *hispanica*) has proved particularly tolerant of urban conditions and is widely planted in London and elsewhere in the temperate world.

Historical type of personal body armor made of bronze, iron or steel plates. Full plate steel armor developed in Europe during the Late Middle Ages, especially in the context of the [[Hundred Years' War|Hundred Years' War]], evolving from a coat of plates worn over mail. Full plate reached its peak in the 15th and 16th centuries, and the complete suit, or panoply, is a feature of the end of the [[Middle Ages|Middle Ages]] and the [[Renaissance|Renaissance]]. The image of the medieval knight comes largely from specialized jousting armor of the 16th century. Heavy cavalry wore the heaviest armor, while some infantry wore lighter three-quarter suits. Use declined in the early 17th century, and after the mid-17th century plate was mostly reduced to the breastplate, or cuirass, because of its weight and because the [[Musket|musket]] could penetrate common armor at range. Mail, made of interlinked iron or steel rings, was worn from the 9th to the 14th centuries. A complete suit typically weighed 45–55 pounds (20–25 kg).

Broad, mainly flat vessel from which food is served or eaten. Plates are [[Tableware|tableware]], typically circular and raised at the edges by a curving wall or a wider lip. In Western culture and many others, the plate is the typical vessel for food that is not too liquid, whereas bowls serve liquid food. Plates of wood, pottery and metal date to antiquity. Some South and Southeast Asian cultures use leaf plates, while East Asian cultures use bamboo and paper. Modern plates are commonly made of [[Porcelain|porcelain]], bone china, earthenware and stoneware, as well as glass, wood and metal. Disposable plates, usually of plastic or paper pulp, were invented in 1904. Dinner plates measure 9–13 inches (23–33 cm) in diameter. The diameter of a typical dinner plate is estimated to have increased by 65% since 1000 AD. Regular plates returned to fashion at the French court under [[Francis I of France|Francis I]] around 1536.

Area of highland with flat terrain, raised sharply above the surrounding land on at least one side. Also called a high plain or tableland, a plateau often has steep escarpments or hills on one or more sides. Plateaus form through volcanic magma upwelling, [[Lava|lava]] extrusion, tectonic uplift, and [[Erosion|erosion]] by water and [[Glacier|glaciers]]. Lava plateaus include the [[Deccan Plateau|Deccan Plateau]] in India and the Columbia Plateau in the United States. Plateaus are classed as intermontane, piedmont or continental. The [[Tibetan Plateau|Tibetan Plateau]], the highest and largest in the world, averages over 4,500 meters in elevation, and the Antarctic Plateau covers most of East Antarctica. The Piedmont Plateau lies between the [[Appalachian Mountains|Appalachian Mountains]] and the Atlantic Plain. The Ethiopian Highlands, the highest African plateau, have little of their surface below 1,500 metres (4,921 ft).

Dense, malleable, precious [[Transition metal|transition metal]] with symbol Pt and atomic number 78. Its name derives from Spanish *platina*, a diminutive of *plata*, meaning silver. It is highly unreactive and does not corrode, even at high temperatures, which makes it a noble metal. Platinum has six naturally occurring isotopes. It is one of the rarer elements in Earth's crust, averaging about 5 μg/kg, and it occurs in some [[Nickel|nickel]] and [[Copper|copper]] ores as well as native deposits. Pre-Columbian South American peoples used it in artifacts, and Antonio de Ulloa reported on it in 1748. Platinum is used in [[Catalytic converter|catalytic converters]], laboratory equipment, electrical contacts, [[Dentistry|dentistry]] and jewelry, and in the glass industry. Compounds such as cisplatin, oxaliplatin and carboplatin are used in [[Chemotherapy|chemotherapy]]. In 2007 Gerhard Ertl won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for determining the mechanisms of catalytic oxidation of carbon monoxide over platinum.

Any of the five convex regular polyhedra in three-dimensional space. Each has congruent regular polygonal faces, with the same number of faces meeting at every vertex: the [[Tetrahedron|tetrahedron]] (four triangular faces), [[Cube|cube]] (six square faces), octahedron (eight triangular faces), [[Dodecahedron|dodecahedron]] (twelve pentagonal faces) and icosahedron (twenty triangular faces). [[Plato|Plato]] associated four of them with the classical elements in his dialogue *Timaeus*. [[Euclid|Euclid]] described all five in Book XIII of his *Elements* and argued that no others exist.

Semiaquatic, egg-laying mammal of eastern [[Australia|Australia]], including [[Tasmania|Tasmania]]. The platypus (*Ornithorhynchus anatinus*) is the sole living member of its family and genus. With the four species of [[Echidna|echidna]], it is one of five living [[Monotreme|monotremes]]. It detects prey electrically while its eyes, ears and nostrils are closed, and males have venomous spurs on their hind feet. In 1799 scientists who examined the first preserved specimen judged it a fake made of several animals sewn together. Hunted for its fur, the platypus has been legally protected since 1912. The IUCN classifies it as near threatened, and a November 2020 report recommended upgrading it to threatened under the federal EPBC Act because of habitat destruction and declining numbers. Its diet consists mainly of aquatic invertebrates.

Roman comic playwright of the Old Latin period. Titus Maccius Plautus is believed to have been born in Sarsina, in what is now [[Emilia-Romagna|Emilia-Romagna]], and he reportedly worked as a stage carpenter before becoming an actor. His comedies, written between about 205 and 184 BC, are the earliest complete surviving works of [[Latin literature|Latin literature]]. They adapt Greek New Comedy, especially the work of Menander, reworking it for Roman audiences. Surviving plays include *Amphitruo*, *Asinaria* and *Menaechmi*. Shakespeare's *The Comedy of Errors* derives from *Menaechmi*, and [[Molière|Molière]]'s *The Miser* is partly modeled on *Aulularia*.

Sixth-generation home video game console by Sony. Released in Japan on March 4, 2000, it succeeded the original [[PlayStation (console)|PlayStation]] and was fully backward compatible with its games. A built-in DVD drive and a custom Emotion Engine processor set it apart. It sold 160 million units, the best-selling console of all time and nearly triple the combined sales of its sixth-generation rivals, [[Nintendo|Nintendo]]'s GameCube, Sega's Dreamcast and Microsoft's Xbox. It was discontinued on January 4, 2013.

Seventh-generation home video game console by Sony. Released in Japan on November 11, 2006, and in North America on November 17, the PS3 was built around the Cell Broadband Engine processor, co-developed with IBM and Toshiba. It was the first console to use [[Blu-ray|Blu-ray]] as its primary storage medium, which helped Sony establish the format over HD DVD. Its high price and costly production hurt early sales. Later revisions reduced costs. The PS3 sold about 87.4 million units worldwide, narrowly surpassing the [[Xbox 360|Xbox 360]]. Final production for Japan ended on May 29, 2017.

Video gaming brand of [[Sony|Sony]] Interactive Entertainment, a Sony subsidiary. It began with the first PlayStation console, released in Japan in 1994 and worldwide the following year, conceived by Sony executive Ken Kutaragi. The original console was the first console of any type to ship over 100 million units. The brand includes handheld consoles, the PlayStation Network and PlayStation Store, the subscription service PlayStation Plus, and first-party games from PlayStation Studios. Its controllers are the DualShock line. The series includes the [[PlayStation 5|PlayStation 5]], released in 2020.

Eighth-generation home video game console by Sony Interactive Entertainment. Released in North America on November 15, 2013, and in Japan on February 22, 2014, it used an [[AMD|AMD]] APU with a theoretical peak of 1.84 teraflops. It added Remote Play and Share Play, which lets others control a player's gameplay remotely. A smaller revision and the high-end PlayStation 4 Pro were released in September 2016. By October 2019 it was the second best-selling PlayStation console of all time, behind the [[PlayStation 2|PlayStation 2]]. It was succeeded by the [[PlayStation 5|PlayStation 5]] in November 2020.

Ninth-generation home video game console by Sony Interactive Entertainment. Announced in April 2019 as the successor to the [[PlayStation 4|PlayStation 4]], it launched on November 12, 2020, in several countries and worldwide a week later. Its hardware includes a solid-state drive for fast data streaming, an [[AMD|AMD]] GPU capable of 4K at up to 120 frames per second, hardware ray tracing, and the DualSense controller with haptic feedback. A PlayStation 5 Pro, released on November 7, 2024, added a faster GPU and AI-driven upscaling. As of June 30, 2026, 95.3 million units had shipped, surpassing the [[PlayStation 3|PlayStation 3]].

Handheld game console by Sony, the first handheld in the PlayStation line. Released in Japan on December 12, 2004, and in North America on March 24, 2005, it was the most powerful portable game console of its time and the first viable competitor to [[Nintendo|Nintendo]]'s handhelds. It used the Universal Media Disc, the only handheld to use an optical disc as its primary storage medium. It also played video, audio and photos, leading some to classify it as a portable media player. It sold over 80 million units during its ten-year lifetime, the best-selling handheld not made by Nintendo. Hardware shipments ended worldwide in 2014.

Fifth-generation home video game console by Sony Computer Entertainment. Released in Japan on December 3, 1994, and in North America and Europe in 1995, it primarily competed with the [[Nintendo 64|Nintendo 64]] and [[Sega Saturn|Sega Saturn]]. Its use of [[Compact disc|compact discs]] marked the game industry's transition from cartridges. Ken Kutaragi designed it with an emphasis on 3D polygon graphics, and it was popular for its low retail price, extensive library and youth marketing. More than 4,000 games were released for it, with cumulative sales of 962 million units. Sony ceased production on March 23, 2006, and the PlayStation became the first computer entertainment platform to ship over 100 million units.
